claim: Force profile analysis (FPA) uses translational arrest peptides (APs) engineered into a target protein to measure the force exerted on a nascent polypeptide chain during translation.
source: We have shown that force profile analysis (FPA) – a method in which a translational arrest peptide (AP) engineered into a target protein serves as a sensor to measure the force exerted on a nascent polypeptide chain during translation – can be used to follow the cotranslational folding of soluble proteins and the membrane integration of a model TMH (Ismail et al., 2012; Ismail et al., 2015; Farías-Rico et al., 2018).
evidence: The text explicitly describes the FPA method and cites previous work demonstrating its use.

claim: FPA can be used to follow the cotranslational folding of soluble proteins and the membrane integration of transmembrane helices.
source: We have shown that force profile analysis (FPA) – a method in which a translational arrest peptide (AP) engineered into a target protein serves as a sensor to measure the force exerted on a nascent polypeptide chain during translation – can be used to follow the cotranslational folding of soluble proteins and the membrane integration of a model TMH (Ismail et al., 2012; Ismail et al., 2015; Farías-Rico et al., 2018).
evidence: The text explicitly states the applications of FPA and cites supporting studies.

claim: Arrest peptides bind in the upper parts of the ribosome exit tunnel and pause translation when their last codon is in the ribosomal A-site.
source: FPA takes advantage of the ability of APs to bind in the upper parts of the ribosome exit tunnel and thereby pause translation when their last codon is in the ribosomal A-site (Ito and Chiba, 2013).
evidence: The text explicitly describes the mechanism of AP-induced pausing and cites a supporting reference.

claim: The duration of an AP-induced pause is reduced in proportion to pulling forces exerted on the nascent chain.
source: The duration of an AP-induced pause is reduced in proportion to pulling forces exerted on the nascent chain (Goldman et al., 2015; Kemp et al., 2020), that is, APs can act as force sensors and can be tuned by mutation to react to different force levels (Cymer et al., 2015a).
evidence: The text explicitly states this relationship and cites supporting studies.

claim: Arrest peptides can act as force sensors and can be tuned by mutation to react to different force levels.
source: The duration of an AP-induced pause is reduced in proportion to pulling forces exerted on the nascent chain (Goldman et al., 2015; Kemp et al., 2020), that is, APs can act as force sensors and can be tuned by mutation to react to different force levels (Cymer et al., 2015a).
evidence: The text explicitly describes the tunability of APs and cites a supporting reference.

claim: The fraction full-length protein produced (fFL) can be used as a proxy for the pulling force F in a given construct.
source: The fraction full-length protein produced, fFL = IFL/(IFL+IA), where IFL and IA are the intensities of the bands representing the full-length (FL) and arrested (A) species on an SDS-PAGE gel (Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), can therefore be used as a proxy for F in a given construct (Kemp et al., 2020; Niesen et al., 2018; Leininger et al., 2019).
evidence: The text explicitly states this relationship and cites supporting studies.

claim: Force profiles can be recorded with up to single-residue resolution by increasing N in steps of one residue.
source: FPs can be recorded with up to single-residue resolution by increasing N in steps of one residue (corresponding to a lengthening of the nascent chain by ~3 Å).
evidence: The text explicitly describes the resolution achievable with FPA.

claim: EmrE is a dual-topology protein with monomers integrating into the inner membrane in a 50-50 mixture of Nin-Cin and Nout-Cout topologies.
source: EmrE is a dual-topology protein, that is, the monomers integrate into the inner membrane in a 50–50 mixture of Nin-Cin and Nout-Cout topologies; two oppositely oriented monomers then assemble into an antiparallel dimer (Chen et al., 2007; Rapp et al., 2007).
evidence: The text explicitly describes EmrE's dual topology and cites supporting references.

claim: Two oppositely oriented EmrE monomers assemble into an antiparallel dimer.

evidence: The text explicitly describes the assembly of EmrE dimers and cites supporting references.

claim: A model TMH composed of Ala and Leu residues generates a peak in an FP that reaches half-maximal amplitude when the N-terminal end of the TMH is ~45 residues away from the polypeptide transferase center.
source: We have previously shown that a model TMH composed of Ala and Leu residues generates a peak in an FP recorded with the SecM(Ec) AP that reaches half-maximal amplitude (Nstart) when the N-terminal end of the TMH is ~45 residues away from the polypeptide transferase center (PTC) (Ismail et al., 2012), and a recent real-time FRET study of cotranslational membrane integration found that the N-terminal end of the first TMH in a protein reaches the vicinity of the SecYEG translocon when it is 40–50 residues away from the PTC (Mercier et al., 2020).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding from previous work and cites the supporting study.

claim: The N-terminal end of the first TMH in a protein reaches the vicinity of the SecYEG translocon when it is 40-50 residues away from the PTC.

claim: GlpG is a medium-sized monomeric 6-TMH rhomboid protease with an ~60 residue cytoplasmic N-terminal domain.
source: We next studied GlpG, a medium-sized monomeric 6-TMH rhomboid protease with an ~60 residue cytoplasmic N-terminal domain (NTD) (Sherratt et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2006) (Figure 3a), a protein that allows us to follow the cotranslational folding of a soluble domain and integration of a membrane domain in the same experiment.
evidence: The text explicitly describes GlpG's structure and cites supporting references.

claim: Peak I in the GlpG force profile at Nstart ≈ 84 residues represents folding of the N-terminal domain.
source: Peak I, at Nstart ≈ 84 residues, is conspicuously close to what would be expected for the folding of the NTD from previous studies of cotranslational folding of small globular domains in the ribosome exit tunnel (Farías-Rico et al., 2018). To verify that the peak indeed represents folding of the NTD, we recorded an FP for the NTD by in vitro transcription-translation in the PURE system (Shimizu et al., 2005) and further made a destabilizing point mutation (F16E) in the core of the NTD (Figure 3c). The FP obtained in vitro (magenta) overlaps peak I in the in vivo FP, and the mutation strongly reduces fFL values for peak I both in vivo (green) and in vitro (black).
evidence: The text explicitly describes the experimental verification of this assignment.

claim: The F16E mutation in the GlpG N-terminal domain strongly reduces fFL values for peak I both in vivo and in vitro.
source: To verify that the peak indeed represents folding of the NTD, we recorded an FP for the NTD by in vitro transcription-translation in the PURE system (Shimizu et al., 2005) and further made a destabilizing point mutation (F16E) in the core of the NTD (Figure 3c). The FP obtained in vitro (magenta) overlaps peak I in the in vivo FP, and the mutation strongly reduces fFL values for peak I both in vivo (green) and in vitro (black).
evidence: The text explicitly describes the experimental result.

claim: The GlpG N-terminal domain has a relative contact order of 15% and is predicted to fold on the ms time scale.
source: Given that the NTD has a relative contact order of 15% and is predicted to fold on the ms time scale (Plaxco et al., 1998) while the elongation cycle on the ribosome takes ~100 ms/codon (Young and Bremer, 1976), the NTD has ample time to equilibrate between the unfolded and accessible folded states at each elongation step (Kemp et al., 2019).
evidence: The text explicitly states this prediction and cites supporting references.
